In this milieu, I agree that the Secretary was summoned to focus on 
these realities. The Act directs the Secretary to consider, among other 
things, whether standards he proposes are “practicable,” and as the 
legislative history denotes, it does not suffice to view merely the 
“technological abihty to achieve the goal of a particular standard.” 
“[EJconomic factors” as well must be scrutinized, and these incIndA 
“reasonableness of cost” and “feasibility.” * * *
*   One may search the record before us for acceptable support for 
the Secretary’s conclusion that the test of practicality was met, but 
the search will be in vain. That, in my view, is the fatal flaw in the 
Secretary’s case.

3. 
Judicial Scrutiny of the Legislature’s Judgments. The inference is 
strong that the retreaders’ primary objections were to the size and maximum 
load requirements which, as the Secretary acknowledged, may preclude pre-
sorting of casings into large groups. But these parts of the rule are upheld. The 
court’s laconic ‘"No rule of administrative law applies to acts of Congress” 
underscores the vast difference between the APA (under which courts closely 
scrutinize the rationality of agency rules while doing nothing to scrutinize the 
rationality of statutory provisions) and the constitutional doctrine of economic 
substantive due process (under which courts scrutinize rationality the same 
for statutory provisions as for the agency rules promulgated thereunder, see 
Pacific States Box & Basket Co. v. White, 296 U.S. 176, 185-86 (1935)).
Following over a decade of seminal court of appeals decisions seeming to 
re-cahbrate the judicial role in reviewing agency rules, the Supreme Court 
finally addressed, in the following opinion, the question of how rigorously 
federal courts should be reviewing agency regulations under the APA.
